data.title: Choose the correct answer for each question.
data.description: Practise nuanced future choices including will, going to, Present Continuous, Present Simple, Future Continuous and Future Perfect.
learningPoints: Use Present Continuous for personal arrangements.
Use Present Simple for timetables and schedules.
Use going to for prior intentions and evidence-based predictions.
Use will for spontaneous decisions and neutral predictions.
Use Future Continuous for actions in progress at a future time.
Use Future Perfect for actions completed before a future deadline.

sections.summary: Using Present Continuous for an arrangement.
sections.explain: Use the Present Continuous for a fixed personal arrangement.

words.word: I'm meeting Sara at six tomorrow.
I meet Sara at six tomorrow, as a personal arrangement with no timetable meaning.
I'll meeting Sara at six tomorrow.

sections.summary: Using Present Simple for a timetable.
sections.explain: Use the Present Simple for scheduled public events and timetables.

words.word: The train leaves at 07:45 tomorrow.
The train is leaving at 07:45 tomorrow because all timetables require continuous.
The train will leaves at 07:45 tomorrow.

sections.explain: Use GOING TO when there is present evidence for a future result.

words.word: Look at those clouds. It's going to rain.
Look at those clouds. It will rain because 'will' is always required for evidence.
Look at those clouds. It's going rain.

sections.explain: Use WILL for a decision made at the moment of speaking.

words.word: The phone's ringing. I'll answer it.
The phone's ringing. I'm going to answer it, expressing a long-standing plan.
The phone's ringing. I'll answering it.

sections.summary: Using Future Continuous for a future activity in progress.
sections.explain: Use WILL BE + verb-ing for an activity in progress at a specified future time.

words.word: At this time tomorrow, we'll be flying over France.
At this time tomorrow, we'll have flown over France if the action is still in progress.
At this time tomorrow, we'll be fly over France.

sections.explain: Use WILL HAVE + past participle for an action completed before a future point.

words.word: By next June, she will have completed the course.
By next June, she will be completing the course, with completed-before-deadline meaning.
By next June, she will have complete the course.

sections.summary: Using a future time clause without 'will'.
sections.explain: After WHEN, BEFORE, AFTER and similar time conjunctions, use a present form for future reference.

words.word: I'll call you when I arrive.
I'll call you when I will arrive.
I'll call you when I arrived tomorrow.

sections.summary: Using 'be about to' for the immediate future.
sections.explain: BE ABOUT TO describes something expected to happen very soon.

words.word: The film is about to start.
The film about to starts.
The film will about start.

sections.explain: BE LIKELY TO expresses probability about the future.

words.word: Prices are likely to rise next year.
Prices likely rise next year are.
Prices are likely rising next year.

sections.explain: Future forms differ according to arrangement, schedule, intention, prediction and completion.

words.word: We're having dinner with them on Friday; the restaurant opens at seven.
We have dinner with them on Friday as a personal arrangement; the restaurant is opening at seven as a timetable.
We're have dinner with them on Friday; the restaurant will opens at seven.
